Documentation → FortiWeb: Policies & Protection → Naming

Naming scheme and discovery

One list of object types per product — every table the device sync reads — with the name pattern of each (the FortiWeb entries are how SATOM names what it creates), and Discovery, which reads the names already on the devices, shows the convention behind them and lets you adopt it as found or adapt it first.

👤 ForAdministrator
🔑 Permissionsusers.manage
📍 WhereEvery device ADOM → Administrator → Naming. Scheme tab (URL /naming/?product=<product>) and Discovery tab (URL /naming/discovery?product=<product>)

ℹ️Note

New: Scheme and Discovery list the same object types in every device ADOM (FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiGate, FortiAuthenticator, FortiAnalyzer) — every table the device sync reads, including the ones no device has an object of yet. Discovery's Adopt writes a found pattern into the scheme; Adopt & adapt lets you change it first. See Discovery.

ℹ️Note

New: patterns SATOM builds names from also take {host} and {port}, and each product has its own Variables: regular-expression rewrites of a token, so blabla.example.com on port 443 can become blabla_example_com-443. See Variables.

What is it?#

The Naming Scheme page holds one name pattern per kind of object (server policy, virtual server, server pool, Web Protection Profile, certificate, and so on). A pattern contains the token {name}. When SATOM derives a name, it replaces the token with a cleaned-up form of a web address or policy name. For example, pol-{name} with shop.example.com gives pol-shop-example-com.

The patterns are team convention, so they live in configuration rather than in code. Each product has its own list and its own stored patterns.

The list has two parts:

  • The catalog (FortiWeb and FortiADC, below) — the objects SATOM names itself. The FortiWeb entries are marked builds names: SATOM fills them in when it creates objects, so they take the site tokens {name}, {host}, {port} and the product's variables only (Managed Certificate: its cert tokens; Exception WPP: {name}). Another token would reach the device as literal text, and Save refuses it.
  • Every other object type the product's configuration sync reads (FortiWeb about 250, FortiADC about 180, and the FortiGate, FortiAuthenticator and FortiAnalyzer tables). These document your convention and are checked against the existing names; they may use any Discovery token ({port}, {proto}, {adom}, {num}, …). A type no device holds an object of yet is listed too ("no objects on any device yet"). Settings blocks are left out: they are not object types. That covers rows without a name, and an empty endpoint the API library measured as one settings object on your devices' builds, or that the FortiAnalyzer / FortiAuthenticator sync saw answer as one object (those syncs record whether each table answered a list, even an empty one, or one object). When nothing has measured an empty type's shape yet, it stays listed and is marked "list or settings block not measured". A table whose objects are keyed by number is listed and marked "keyed by number on the devices", so the two tabs always show the same object types.

What does it do?#

  • Lists every object type of the selected product, grouped by section, with its current pattern and a live preview (→ result) computed from a Sample web address (other tokens get sample values: {port} → 443, {proto} → https, {adom} → root).
  • Shows under each input what Discovery found on the devices (all devices agree, devices differ, or the one device), a use it link that copies it in, and a live count of the existing names that follow your pattern.
  • A filter box and Only types with objects on a device narrow the list.
  • Saves your patterns as overrides. An empty field means "use the default pattern" (the default is shown as the field's placeholder).
  • Restore defaults discards every override of the selected product.
  • Writes an audit entry (naming.save) for every save and reset.

The catalog#

Product Section Objects (default pattern)
FortiWeb Server Policy Server Policy (pol-{name}), Virtual Server (vs-{name}), Virtual IP (VIP) (vip-{name}), Server Pool (pool-{name}), Health Check (hc-{name}), Persistence (persist-{name}), Content Routing (cr-{name}), Session cookie (FWB-{name}), Local certificate (cert-{name})
FortiWeb Web Protection Profile Web Protection Profile (wpp-{name}), HTTP Protocol Constraints, X-Forwarded-For, Allow Method, IP List, Geo Block List, Cookie Security, CSRF Protection, Padding Oracle, HTTP Header Security, Parameter Validation, Hidden Fields, File Upload, URL Access, Bot Mitigation (each <prefix>-{name}), Exception WPP (per-policy clone) (wpp-{name})
FortiWeb Certificate Manager Managed Certificate (cert-{class}-{cn}-{date})
FortiADC Server Load Balance Virtual Server, Real Server, Real Server Pool, Health Check, Persistence, Load Balance Method, Content Routing, Content Rewriting, Schedule Pool, Error Page
FortiADC SSL Client SSL Profile, Server SSL Profile, Local certificate

Hover over a field to see its note, where one exists. For example, the note on Exception WPP (per-policy clone) explains that {name} is the server policy's name there, not a web address.

Where the patterns are used#

Consumer Pattern it reads Honors your overrides?
Exceptions: the per-policy clone of a template-managed Web Protection Profile Exception WPP (per-policy clone) Yes
Certificate Manager: the name of a managed certificate Managed Certificate (tokens {class}, {cn}, {date}, {serial}) Yes
New Server Policy from a line: names of the policy, virtual server, pool, VIP and related objects the Server Policy section (FortiWeb) Yes

ℹ️Note

Changed in 2.11.0: the line wizard now names its objects with the FortiWeb patterns saved on this page; before, it always used the built-in defaults.

If a pattern renders an empty name for an object the wizard needs, the wizard plan is blocked with the naming scheme produced no name for: <keys> — fix it in Administrator -> Naming.

The FortiADC catalog is stored and editable, with its own variables that work exactly like FortiWeb's, but no FortiADC workflow in this release derives names from it yet; a flow that does uses the same patterns and variables unchanged.

If a derived name holds a character the devices refuse (anything but letters, digits, _ and -, typically a dot from {host}), the wizard plan is blocked with naming_unsafe, naming the object and the character.

Requirements#

  • Nothing beyond the permission. Patterns can be set before any device is registered.

Permissions#

users.manage is required to open and save the page (Administrator). The page is admin-only through the legacy user_manage gate, which only users.manage grants. Users without it don't see the Administrator menu group, and opening /naming/ directly returns 403 Forbidden.

The page opens from any ADOM, including Global (for example through the Naming link on the Exceptions page or a bookmark). Before 2.11.0 it answered with a server error (HTTP 500) while the Global ADOM was active.

How to use#

Edit the patterns of one product#

  1. Open Administrator → Naming in the FortiWeb ADOM. From the FortiADC ADOM's Administrator → Naming, the page opens on FortiADC.
  2. Pick the product in the Product selector at the top right of the Patterns card. The page reloads with that product's catalog.
  3. Type a realistic address into Sample web address (default shop.example.com) and a Port (default 443). The hint shows what {name}, {host} and {port} become, and every row shows its result after →, computed by the server with the variables on the page.
  4. Change the patterns you want. Leave a field empty to keep its default.
  5. Click Save Naming. The flash reads FortiWeb naming patterns saved. (or FortiADC …).

Return to the defaults#

  1. Select the product.
  2. Click Restore defaults. The flash reads <product> naming patterns restored to defaults (variables kept). The variables are not reset; remove them in the table.

Configuration#

Field Description Required Example
Product Which product's object types are shown and saved. Every device ADOM is listed Yes FortiWeb
Sample web address, Port Preview inputs only; never stored No shop.example.com, 443
Variables Per product, in order: name, the token it reads, a regular expression, what to replace with No host_u · host · \. · _
pattern per object type builds names entries: text with {name}, {host}, {port} and the variables. Other entries: any Discovery token. Empty = the default pattern (catalog) or no pattern No pol-{name}, {host_u}-{port}, hc-{proto}-{name}
Managed Certificate Uses {class}, {cn}, {date}, {serial} instead of {name} No cert-{class}-{cn}-{date}

How {name} is derived: the address is lower-cased, and the scheme (https://), port, path and query are dropped. Every run of characters other than a–z and 0–9 becomes a single -, and leading and trailing dashes are removed. https://Shop.Example.com:8443/cart?x=1 becomes shop-example-com. Derived names are cut at 63 characters.

Token Value for https://Blabla.Example.com:8443/x
{name} blabla-example-com
{host} blabla.example.com (host as typed, lower-cased, dots kept)
{port} the port the creating flow gives (the wizard's Port column, or port in its API body); else 8443 from the address; the wizard falls back to 443 with a certificate, 80 without

Variables#

A variable turns a token into the text a name needs. The table sits above the patterns and belongs to the selected product.

  1. Press Add variable.
  2. Name: lower-case letters, digits and _, starting with a letter (at most 32). The names SATOM and Discovery already use (name, host, port, class, cn, date, serial, proto, adom, vdom, num, ip, device) are refused.
  3. Reads: name, host, port or a variable above this one.
  4. Regular expression and Replace with: Python re.sub — every match is replaced, \1 refers to a group.
  5. The Sample value column shows the result for the sample address. Use the variable in any pattern as {its_name} and press Save Naming: variables and patterns are saved together and checked together.
Variable Reads Regular expression Replace with blabla.example.com →
host_u host \. _ blabla_example_com
sub host ^([^.]+)\..*$ \1 blabla
short host_u _example_com$ (empty) blabla

With Server Policy = {host_u}-{port} and port 443, the wizard names the policy blabla_example_com-443.

Nothing is saved when a variable cannot be computed (reserved name, a source that is not a token or a variable above it, a regular expression that does not compile, a \2 with one group, more than 20 variables), and a save that removes a variable a pattern still uses is refused with the pattern named. Existing names are checked against a catalog pattern with {host} and the variables read as free text, so blabla_example_com-443 follows {host_u}-{port}.

Example#

🧪Example — A team prefix for every policy object

Your convention is fw-<site>-<type>. Set Server Policy to fw-{name}-pol, Server Pool to fw-{name}-pool and Exception WPP (per-policy clone) to fw-{name}-wpp. With the sample shop.example.com the preview shows fw-shop-example-com-pol and fw-shop-example-com-pool. When an operator later needs a carve-out on a template-managed profile for policy shop, the Exceptions page creates the clone fw-shop-wpp.

Result#

  • Only non-empty fields are stored, per product. A cleared field reverts to its default at once.
  • New names are derived from the new patterns from the next operation on. Existing objects on appliances are never renamed.
  • The Audit Log records naming.save with the number of stored patterns, or Reset … naming to defaults.

Discovery#

The scheme above says how new objects are named. Discovery reads the names that are already on a device and shows, for every object type, the convention behind them. It reads the configuration tree SATOM keeps for each device (the same read-only sweep the other pages use); it never contacts the device unless you press Sync device.

What each row shows#

Column Meaning
Object type The table as the ADOM's own menu labels it, its section and its registry name
Convention found The dominant pattern, then any variant (another prefix used by part of the objects), the separator and the letter case
Follow it How many of the team's objects match the pattern (green ≥ 90 %, amber ≥ 60 %, red below)
Naming scheme The scheme pattern of this object type and how many objects follow it; (default) when it is the catalog default
Shares {name} with Object types that carry the same identifier through a real reference (a policy → its pool → its virtual server)
Vendor Factory objects of this type, excluded from everything (hover for the reason)

Open the line under a row for the exceptions, each with its reason, and for every name.

How a pattern is built#

A name is split on -, _, . and spaces. Each part becomes:

  • literal — the same text on (nearly) every object: pol;
  • a field token — the part equals a field of the same object, or the device's ADOM/VDOM or name, on at least 80 % of the objects: {port}, {proto} (a service word such as https, also matched against the port), {adom}, {device}, {host}, {ip}, or the field's own name;
  • {num} — digits that match no field;
  • {name} — the free part, the site identifier. It is the scheme's own token.

Comments and descriptions are never matched (they repeat the name's words). One object alone is not a convention: the row says "too few".

The exceptions you want to read first#

  • Stale names — name says 'https' but the object's port is '8080' — stale name?: the name stopped describing the object.
  • A variant prefix, a prefix no other object uses, a single word where the others have parts, a different separator.

Vendor objects#

Factory objects say nothing about your convention, so they are counted apart. SATOM uses the device's own flag first — FortiWeb can_view=1, FortiADC _nondeletable=1, FortiGate q_static and the certificate source, FortiAnalyzer protected=1 — then a list of factory names measured on a real unit of each product for the vendor objects a device does not flag (FortiGate's predefined services and addresses, FortiADC's DEFAULT_* objects), then physical port names. The footnote names the unit and build each list was measured on.

Adopt or adapt a convention#

  • Adopt writes the found pattern into the scheme entry of that object type. Every device of the product is then checked against it, and the names that break it are listed under the row. in scheme means the scheme already has that pattern; the ✕ clears the entry.
  • Adopt & adapt opens the pattern in an editor under the row. Change what you need — lab-spo-{num} → spo-{name} — and the count of names that follow updates as you type, with the first names that do not. Save to scheme stores your version. It is offered for every object type with team objects, also when no shared pattern was found.
  • For a builds names entry, Adopt is greyed out when the found pattern has a token SATOM cannot fill in (pol-{adom}-{name}); hover for the reason and use Adopt & adapt.

Fleet view and export#

  • All devices (fleet view) lists each object type with the pattern most devices use, all agree or devices differ, each device's own pattern and coverage, and your scheme pattern (red when it differs from what most devices use).
  • Export CSV writes one line per exception (or per object type without exceptions) for the device or the fleet. Cells are neutralised against spreadsheet formulas.

A device with no configuration tree#

The page says so and offers Sync device (read-only). FortiGate has a tree from this release on: before it, a FortiGate sync ran the FortiWeb sweep and failed every table. The FortiGate sweep reads every table of the FortiGate ADOM menu at the path the registry resolves for the unit's build, and drops secrets exactly like the section pages.

Troubleshooting#

Discovery shows a vendor object as a team object (or the reverse)#

Possible causes - The device does not flag the object and it is not in the measured factory-name list for its product.

Solution 1. Check the row's Vendor tooltip: it names the reason for each excluded object. 2. Report the object; the list lives in app/registry/data/naming_factory.json.

Verification - After an update that adds the name, the object moves to Vendor.

Discovery says the device has no configuration tree#

Possible causes - The device was never synced, or every table failed on its last sync (the previous tree is kept).

Solution 1. Click Sync device. The flash shows the sync summary.

Verification - The page shows the object types and "Configuration read UTC".

Objects created by the line wizard do not use my patterns#

Possible causes - The patterns were saved for FortiADC, not FortiWeb. The wizard reads the FortiWeb catalog. - The plan was computed before you saved the patterns.

Solution 1. Select FortiWeb in the Product selector, check the patterns and click Save Naming. 2. Run the wizard's plan again.

Verification - In the wizard's preview, Device payloads show the new pool's name rendered with your Server Pool pattern.

The FortiADC ADOM shows FortiWeb patterns#

Possible causes - The page was opened without ?product=fortiadc. An unknown or missing product falls back to FortiWeb.

Solution 1. Use the Product selector, or open /naming/?product=fortiadc.

Verification - The breadcrumb ends in FortiADC, and the card title reads Patterns — FortiADC.

A derived name is cut off#

Possible causes - The rendered name exceeds 63 characters. SATOM truncates it so the appliance accepts it.

Solution 1. Shorten the fixed part of the pattern (prefixes or suffixes), or use shorter web addresses.

Verification - The preview after → shows the full name with no truncation.

Advanced#

Advanced Storage
  • Overrides are stored as JSON in the application settings: key naming.scheme for FortiWeb (the original key, kept for compatibility) and naming.scheme.<product> for other products.
  • The product selector lists every device ADOM.
  • An object type outside the catalog is stored in the same per-product key as table:<registry name>; the flows that build names never read those.
  • The first cut of Discovery kept adopted patterns apart, under naming.discovered.<product>. The page moves them into the scheme the first time it opens (unless the entry already has its own pattern) and logs it. Adopting now writes the audit entry naming.save.
  • The object types come from the product's sync plan (FortiWeb and FortiADC: the sweep plan; FortiGate: the ADOM menu; FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator: the registry of each unit's build), joined with what the stored configuration trees hold.
  • This page (both tabs) is the only writer of the patterns. The former POST /settings/naming endpoint was removed in 2.11.0.
  • The preview runs in the browser. It also substitutes sample values for the certificate tokens ({class} → server, {date} → 20260701, {serial} → a3f1), so the Managed Certificate row previews meaningfully.
